reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: A congenital defect in which the anal opening is absent or abnormally positioned; usually detected on the routine newborn examination or when meconium fails to pass normally
Malformations are broadly grouped as low or high depending on whether the rectal pouch ends below or above the levator ani muscle complex, which guides operative approach and prognosis
Most cases in both sexes involve a fistula connecting the blind rectum to the perineum, urinary tract, or genital tract, and meconium seen at an abnormal site is a useful clue
The condition frequently forms part of the VACTERL group, so vertebral, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies should be actively sought
Initial management is to keep the infant nil by mouth, decompress the stomach, and give intravenous fluids while assessing the level of the lesion
High or complex lesions are typically managed with an initial diverting colostomy followed by definitive posterior sagittal anorectoplasty, whereas some low lesions can be corrected in one stage
Long-term outcome depends heavily on the quality of the sphincter mechanism and sacral development, so continence must be followed over years
A distal colostogram and cross-table lateral radiography help define the anatomy before definitive repair
reference.pathophysiology: Imperforate anus results from abnormal development of the hindgut and its separation from the urogenital sinus during early embryogenesis, so the terminal rectum fails to descend and open normally onto the perineum. The rectal pouch commonly ends blindly or communicates through a fistula with the urinary system, vagina, or perineal skin. The relationship of the pouch to the levator ani and external sphincter complex, together with the degree of sacral and spinal development, determines whether continence structures are adequate and largely predicts functional outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Rectal atresia with a normal-appearing anus
additionalInvestigations: Cross-table lateral prone radiograph (invertogram) to estimate the level of the rectal pouch
Distal colostogram to delineate fistula anatomy prior to definitive surgery
Renal and pelvic ultrasound to detect associated urological anomalies
Echocardiography and spinal imaging as part of a VACTERL screen
Sacral radiographs to assess sacral ratio, which correlates with continence potential
redFlags: Signs of intestinal obstruction (abdominal distension, bilious vomiting) requiring urgent decompression and surgical review
Meconium in the urine indicating a rectourinary fistula and risk of urinary contamination
Associated cardiac or renal anomalies that may destabilise the neonate before surgery
Failure to identify any perineal opening in a distended infant, mandating prompt surgical decompression
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with the type of malformation: low lesions with good sphincter and sacral development often achieve near-normal continence, while high or cloacal lesions carry higher rates of faecal incontinence and constipation requiring long-term bowel management. Associated anomalies significantly influence overall morbidity.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis when a perineal fistula allows some meconium to pass, giving false reassurance
Attempting a primary perineal repair on a high lesion without a protective colostomy
Overlooking associated VACTERL anomalies, particularly cardiac and renal lesions
Underestimating the long-term need for bowel management and continence follow-up
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Initial stabilisation keeping the infant nil by mouth, decompressing the stomach with a nasogastric tube and giving intravenous fluids while the level of the lesion is assessed
Active screening for and management of associated VACTERL anomalies, including cardiac, renal, vertebral and spinal cord abnormalities
A diverting colostomy for high or complex malformations, followed later by definitive posterior sagittal anorectoplasty
Primary single-stage anoplasty for selected low lesions
Postoperative anal dilatations to prevent anastomotic stricture
Long-term bowel management with laxatives, dietary measures or antegrade enemas to address constipation or faecal incontinence
Multidisciplinary follow-up involving paediatric surgery, urology and continence services
